mainTopic: Insulting names for עבודה זרה, and when worshipped natural objects like mountains, plants and fallen stones become forbidden
overview: This amud opens in the middle of a ברייתא. An earlier view on the previous amud read the פסוק 'ואבדתם את שמם' as a command to root out עבודה זרה. רבי עקיבא answers that rooting out is already taught by 'אבד תאבדון', so this פסוק teaches something new: give the idol a new name, and the ברייתא shows that name must be insulting. Next, a ברייתא recited before רב ששת rules that worshipped mountains stay permitted but worshipped plants are forbidden. רב ששת says it follows רבי יוסי בר יהודה. Then בני רבי חייא and רבי יוחנן disagree about worshipped stones that broke off a mountain. The lenient view is explained with a הצד השוה, since nothing made by people is involved, and the strict view with the פסוק 'שקץ תשקצנו'. The גמרא tries to prove from חזקיה's egg question which side בני רבי חייא hold, rejects the proof, and the egg question ends in תיקו. Finally רמי בר חמא asks whether a worshipped mountain's stones may be used for the מזבח.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא points out that the verse looks extra
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא argues that destroying idols is already taught by 'אבד תאבדון', so 'ואבדתם את שמם' must teach something else.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי עקיבא said to him: Wasn't it already said, 'You shall surely destroy'? If so, what does the verse 'And you shall destroy their name out of that place' come to teach?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי עקיבא challenges the earlier reading of the פסוק by showing that the destroying is already taught by a different פסוק. He is setting up his own reading, which comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תורה does not repeat itself for no reason. 'אבד תאבדון' (דברים 12:2) already commands wiping out idols. So 'ואבדתם את שמם' (דברים 12:3) cannot just be saying the same thing again, and it must carry a new lesson.

keyTerms.meaning: But wasn't it already said? (pointing to a פסוק that already teaches this)
What does the verse come to teach?
And you shall destroy their name

phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva said to him:
But wasn't it already stated: "You shall surely destroy"?
If so, what does the verse come to teach when it says:
"And you shall destroy their name out of that place"?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא, וַהֲלֹא כְּבָר נֶאֱמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to the earlier view in the ברייתא, which is not part of this section.
steps.kashyaTarget: The earlier reading that 'ואבדתם את שמם' teaches rooting out idols
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: That lesson is already taught by 'אבד תאבדון', so the second פסוק would be extra.

steps.title: The verse means: give the idol a new name
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא's reading: 'destroying their name' means calling the idol by a different name.
steps.simpleTranslation: It teaches that you should give it a nickname.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי עקיבא gives his own reading of 'ואבדתם את שמם': we must call the idol by a substitute name.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since physically destroying the idol is already covered, 'destroying their name' is read as being about the name itself. You wipe out the idol's real name by replacing it with a different one.

keyTerms.meaning: To give a nickname, to call by a substitute name

phrases.english: To give it a nickname.
phrases.notes: "It" means the עבודה זרה, the idol or its place of worship.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question raised in step 1 about what the extra פסוק teaches.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There is a מצוה to call עבודה זרה by a substitute name.

steps.title: Could the new name be a nice one?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא raises the possibility that the nickname could be a flattering one.
steps.simpleTranslation: One might think: a praising name?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא asks what kind of nickname is meant, and floats the idea that it could even be a complimentary one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 2 only said 'a nickname' and did not say what kind. This line tests the widest possibility before the ברייתא narrows it down.

keyTerms.meaning: One might have thought (introduces a possible mistaken idea)

phrases.english: One might think: a name of praise?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks what kind of nickname step 2 requires.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the substitute name could be a flattering one.

steps.title: The גמרא rejects the idea of a praising name
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא breaks in: how could anyone think you may praise an idol?
steps.simpleTranslation: A praising name? Could that enter your mind?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא interrupts the ברייתא to object that it makes no sense to suggest a complimentary name for an idol.
steps.deeperAnalysis: It is obviously wrong to honor עבודה זרה, so the ברייתא would not need a פסוק to rule this out. That means the 'יכול' in step 3 cannot be read the plain way.

phrases.english: A name of praise, could that enter your mind?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Objects to the wording of step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's suggestion that the nickname might be complimentary
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Praising an idol is plainly forbidden, so no פסוק is needed to rule it out.

steps.title: The real question: maybe a neutral name is enough
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rereads the ברייתא: it was asking whether a neutral name, neither nice nor insulting, would be enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, one might think: a name that is neither praising nor insulting?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the reading of the ברייתא. The real possibility was a neutral nickname.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A neutral name is a reasonable guess, because it still replaces the idol's real name. Now the ברייתא has a real question that a פסוק needs to answer.

phrases.english: Rather, one might think
a name neither of praise nor of insult?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא יָכוֹל לֹא לְשֶׁבַח וְלֹא לִגְנַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 4 by rereading the question of step 3.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא was considering a flattering name.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא was considering a neutral name.

steps.title: A verse shows the name must be insulting
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק 'שקץ תשקצנו ותעב תתעבנו' shows the nickname must be a disgusting, insulting one.
steps.simpleTranslation: The verse teaches: 'You shall utterly detest it and utterly abhor it, for it is a banned thing.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא brings a פסוק to prove that a neutral name is not enough and the name must be insulting.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תורה commands us to detest and abhor עבודה זרה. A neutral name does not show disgust, so the nickname has to be a put-down.
steps.whatToRemember: Following רבי עקיבא: there is a מצוה to call עבודה זרה by a name, and that name must be insulting, not neutral.

phrases.english: The verse teaches:
"You shall utterly detest it
and you shall utterly abhor it,
for it is a banned thing."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rules out the neutral-name possibility raised in step 5.
steps.raayaObject: That the nickname must be insulting
steps.raayaSupportSource: דברים 7:26, 'שקץ תשקצנו ותעב תתעבנו כי חרם הוא'

steps.title: How is this done in practice?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks for a practical example of an insulting nickname.
steps.simpleTranslation: How so?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא asks how this rule actually works. It is setting up the examples in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule has been stated, but we still need to see what such a name looks like.

keyTerms.meaning: How so? How is this carried out?

phrases.english: How so?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for practical examples of the rule from step 6.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What an insulting nickname looks like in practice.

steps.title: Examples: twisting nice names into ugly ones
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא gives examples: בית גליא becomes בית כריא, פני מלך becomes פני כלב, עין כל becomes עין קוץ.
steps.simpleTranslation: If they would call it 'בית גליא' (house of revealing), we call it 'בית כריא' (house of a pit). 'Face of a king' becomes 'face of a dog.' 'All-seeing eye' becomes 'eye of a thorn.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא shows how to do it: take the idol's grand name and change it slightly into something disgraceful.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each new name sounds close to the original but means something shameful. This way the idol's honored name is wiped out and replaced by mockery.

keyTerms.meaning: House of revealing or elevation (the idol's honored name)
House of a pit, house of digging (the insulting name)

phrases.english: If they would call it "Beit Galya" (house of revealing),
we call it "Beit Karya" (house of a pit);
"face of a king" becomes "face of a dog";
"all-seeing eye" becomes "eye of a thorn."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 7 with concrete examples.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Change the idol's honored name into a similar-sounding shameful one.

steps.title: Worshipped mountains are permitted but worshipped plants are forbidden
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא recited before רב ששת: mountains and hills that were worshipped are permitted, but plants and vegetables that were worshipped are forbidden. In both cases the worshippers are killed by the sword.
steps.simpleTranslation: A תנא taught before רב ששת: Gentiles who worship mountains and hills: the mountains and hills are permitted, and their worshippers are killed by the sword. Plants and vegetables: they are forbidden, and their worshippers are killed by the sword.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new topic. It quotes a ברייתא about whether worshipped parts of nature become forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worshippers are equally guilty in both cases, since both get the death penalty by the sword. Still, the objects are treated differently: mountains stay permitted, while plants become forbidden. That difference is what the גמרא will need to explain.

keyTerms.meaning: A tanna taught before רב ששת
Permitted (may be used or benefited from)

steps.confusionAlert: The worshipper's punishment and the status of the object are two separate questions. The mountain being permitted does not mean worshipping it is any less of a sin.

phrases.english: A tanna taught before Rav Sheshet:
phrases.notes: The תנא here is the person in the study hall whose job was to recite ברייתות from memory.

phrases.english: The gentiles who worship
the mountains and the hills:
they are permitted,
and their worshippers are killed by the sword.
And the plants and the vegetables:
they are forbidden,
and their worshippers are killed by the sword.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, unrelated to the nickname discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Worshipped mountains and hills are permitted and worshipped plants and vegetables are forbidden. In both cases the worshippers are put to death by the sword.
steps.whyThisMatters: It sets up the question of why one attached part of nature stays permitted while another becomes forbidden.

steps.title: רב ששת identifies the author of the ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת says the ברייתא that forbids worshipped plants follows רבי יוסי בר יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת said to him: Who taught you this? It is רבי יוסי בר יהודה, who says that a tree that was planted and only later worshipped is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת tells the person who recited the ברייתא which תנא it follows. Plants that are worshipped are forbidden even though they are attached to the ground, and that only fits רבי יוסי בר יהודה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally something attached to the ground does not become forbidden when it is worshipped, which is why mountains stay permitted. The ברייתא still forbids worshipped plants, so רב ששת matches it to רבי יוסי בר יהודה. He holds that a tree planted for a normal reason and later worshipped becomes forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: Who is it? The question asking which תנא taught a statement.
He planted it, and only afterward worshipped it.
Forbidden. Here it means you may not get any benefit from it.

phrases.english: He said to him: The one who told you this, who is he?
It is Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda,
who says: a tree that one planted
and in the end worshipped it is forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains which תנא the ברייתא from Step 9 follows.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Matching the source to a specific תנא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא might seem to go against the usual rule that attached things are not forbidden.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא follows רבי יוסי בר יהודה, who forbids a tree that was planted and later worshipped.

steps.title: Why not read the ברייתא so it fits the רבנן too?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the ברייתא could be about plants planted for worship from the start, so it would fit the רבנן as well.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let us explain the ברייתא as talking about a tree planted from the start for worship, and then it could follow the רבנן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רב ששת. Why tie the ברייתא to one opinion, when it could be read in a way that everyone agrees with?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even the רבנן agree that a tree planted for worship in the first place is forbidden. If the ברייתא is about that kind of plant, there is no need to say it follows only רבי יוסי בר יהודה. The גמרא usually prefers a reading that matches the majority view.

keyTerms.meaning: But let us set it up as. A suggestion to read a source as talking about a specific case.
From the start, for this purpose (worship)

phrases.english: But let us explain it as a tree
that one planted from the start for this purpose,
and then it fits the Rabbis!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב ששת's choice of תנא in Step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ששת's statement that the ברייתא follows only רבי יוסי בר יהודה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A different reading of the case would let the ברייתא fit the majority view, so there is no need to limit it to one תנא.

steps.title: The plants are compared to a mountain, so they were not planted for worship
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא lists plants alongside a mountain, which nobody plants. So the plants too were not planted for worship.
steps.simpleTranslation: Don't think that. The ברייתא teaches the plants together with a mountain. A mountain was not planted for worship from the start, so these plants were also not planted for worship from the start.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the suggestion from Step 11. The way the ברייתא is built shows which kind of plant it means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא puts mountains and plants side by side. So we read the plants to be like the mountain, which no one planted for worship. That means the plants were planted normally and only later worshipped, which only רבי יוסי בר יהודה forbids. So רב ששת's reading stands.

keyTerms.meaning: Don't think that. Literally, it should not come up in your mind.

phrases.english: This cannot enter your mind,
since it teaches it as similar to a mountain;
just as a mountain is something one did not plant
from the start for this purpose,
so too this one also
is something not planted from the start for this purpose.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא סָלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ, דְּקָתָנֵי דּוּמְיָא דְּהַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 11 and supports רב ששת.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Proof from how the ברייתא is structured (the plants are listed alongside the mountain)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא could be about plants planted for worship, which would fit the רבנן.
steps.terutzMaskana: The plants are like the mountain: not planted for worship. So the ברייתא follows only רבי יוסי בר יהודה.
steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא's comparison of plants to a mountain shows it is about plants not planted for worship. That is why רב ששת says it follows רבי יוסי בר יהודה.

steps.title: A disagreement about stones that came loose from a mountain
steps.stepSummary: The sons of רבי חייא and רבי יוחנן disagree about stones that broke off a mountain and were then worshipped. One side says they are forbidden, the other says they are permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: About stones that came loose from a mountain, the sons of רבי חייא and רבי יוחנן disagree. One says they are forbidden, and one says they are permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic: stones that fell off a mountain on their own and were then worshipped. Two sides disagree, and we are not told which side holds which view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A mountain itself stays permitted even if it is worshipped. The question is about stones that broke loose. They are no longer attached to the ground, but no person made or moved them either.

keyTerms.meaning: That came loose and broke off on their own

phrases.english: It was stated: stones of a mountain that came loose,
phrases.notes: The case is that someone worshipped these loose stones.

phrases.english: the sons of Rabbi Chiya and Rabbi Yochanan disagree:
one says: they are forbidden,
and one says: they are permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the ברייתא about mountains and plants to a related case: worshipped stones that broke off a mountain.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There is a מחלוקת whether worshipped stones that came loose from a mountain are forbidden or permitted.

steps.title: Why would the loose stones be permitted?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason behind the lenient view.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason of the one who says they are permitted?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the logic behind the view that the loose stones are permitted. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Loose stones are no longer attached to the ground, so you might expect them to be forbidden like any other worshipped object. The גמרא wants to know why one side permits them.

phrases.english: What is the reason of the one who says they are permitted?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind one side of the disagreement in Step 13.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason the loose stones would stay permitted after being worshipped

steps.title: The stones are like the mountain because no person made them
steps.stepSummary: The stones are compared to a mountain: neither one came about through human effort, so both are permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: They are like a mountain. A mountain was not handled by human hands, and it is permitted. So too these stones were not handled by human hands, and they are permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the lenient view. The loose stones are like the mountain they came from.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The key idea is that no person had a hand in making the thing. The mountain is permitted because no person had a hand in making it, and the stones broke off by themselves, so they share that same feature.

keyTerms.meaning: Human handling. The thing came about through a person's effort.

phrases.english: Like a mountain:
just as a mountain has in it no
human handling, and it is permitted,
so too these, which have in them no
human handling, are permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּהַר — מָה הַר שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ תְּפִיסַת יְדֵי אָדָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 14.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The stones are like the mountain. Neither came about through human effort, so both stay permitted.

steps.title: But a mountain is attached to the ground
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the comparison: maybe the mountain is permitted because it is attached to the ground, and loose stones are not attached.
steps.simpleTranslation: What about a mountain? It is special because it is attached to the ground!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the comparison from Step 15. It points out a difference between a mountain and loose stones.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Maybe the real reason a mountain is permitted is that it is attached to the ground, not that no person made it. If so, loose stones, which are detached, cannot learn from the mountain.

keyTerms.meaning: What about a mountain? This points to something special about it.

phrases.english: What about a mountain? It is special because it is attached!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the comparison to a mountain from Step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: The comparison of loose stones to a mountain
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A mountain has a special feature, being attached to the ground, which the loose stones lack. So the leniency may not carry over.

steps.title: An animal proves that being attached is not the reason
steps.stepSummary: A worshipped animal is permitted even though it is not attached to the ground. So being attached is not what makes something permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: An animal will prove it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge with the case of an animal. An animal is not attached to the ground, yet it does not become forbidden when it is worshipped.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If being attached were the only reason for the leniency, a worshipped animal should be forbidden. It is permitted, though, so the common factor must be that no person made it. That brings back the comparison of the stones to the mountain.

keyTerms.meaning: Will prove it. This brings a case that knocks out the suggested difference.

steps.confusionAlert: This step is not saying that an animal is the same as a mountain in every way. It only shows that being attached to the ground is not the reason for the leniency.

phrases.english: An animal will prove it.
phrases.notes: He means a worshipped animal is permitted even though it isn't attached to the ground, so being attached can't be the reason.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Pushes away the challenge of Step 16 and brings back the comparison of Step 15.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A second case that knocks out the suggested difference
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The mountain is permitted only because it is attached to the ground.
steps.terutzMaskana: An animal is not attached and is still permitted. So the shared reason is that no person made it, and the loose stones share that.
steps.whatToRemember: For the lenient view, the key is that no person made the thing. The animal case is challenged right away in the next step, and the proof is rebuilt as a הצד השוה in step 20.

steps.title: An animal is different because it is alive
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back on the animal proof: maybe a worshipped animal is permitted only because it is a living creature, and stones are not alive.
steps.simpleTranslation: What about an animal? It is different, because it is a living creature!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the proof from step 17. It says an animal might be permitted for its own special reason: it is alive.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 17 used a worshipped animal to show that being attached to the ground is not the reason something stays permitted. Now the גמרא says the animal has its own feature, being alive, that stones do not have. So the animal cannot teach us about stones either.

keyTerms.meaning: What about...? The standard way to point out what makes a case different

phrases.english: What about an animal?
It is different, since it is a living creature!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the animal proof brought in step 17.
steps.kashyaTarget: Using a worshipped animal as proof that loose stones are permitted.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The animal has its own unique feature (being alive), so it may be permitted for that reason, which does not apply to stones.

steps.title: A mountain proves being alive is not the reason
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that a mountain is not alive and is still permitted, so being alive is not what makes something permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: A mountain will prove it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge with a short reply: look at a mountain. A mountain is not alive, yet a worshipped mountain is permitted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If being alive were the real reason, a mountain would be forbidden. It is not, so being alive cannot be the deciding factor. This reply also sets up the next step, where both cases are combined into one proof.

keyTerms.meaning: will prove; brings a case that knocks down the other side's point

phrases.english: A mountain will prove it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 18 by bringing back the mountain case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Counter-example: a case that lacks the suggested feature but has the same law.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Maybe an animal is permitted only because it is alive.
steps.terutzMaskana: A mountain is not alive and is still permitted, so being alive is not the reason.

steps.title: Building a proof from what the mountain and animal share
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא combines the mountain and the animal. Each has its own weakness, but they share one feature: neither was made by people. So anything not made by people, like the stones, stays permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: The argument has come back around. This case is not like that one, and that case is not like this one. What they have in common is that people did not make them, and they are permitted. So too, anything people did not make is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא uses a הצד השוה, a proof from the common feature of two cases. The mountain and the animal are each different in their own way, but both were not made by people, and both stay permitted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The mountain alone could be rejected because it is attached to the ground. The animal alone could be rejected because it is alive. But each case covers the other's weakness, so all that remains is what they share: no תפיסת ידי אדם. The stones share that feature too, so they should be permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: the argument has come back around; we return to the proof using both cases together
this case is not like that case; each has its own special feature
the common feature shared by two cases
human involvement; something people made or worked on

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the classic הצד השוה method, used all over ש״ס. If you see how two weak proofs cover for each other, you will recognize the pattern everywhere.

phrases.english: And the argument has come back around:
phrases.notes: He means: we started with a mountain, then an animal, and now we use both together.

phrases.english: this case is not like that case,
and that case is not like this case;
phrases.notes: The mountain is attached but not alive, and the animal is alive but not attached.

phrases.english: the common feature between them

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאֵין בָּהֶן תְּפִיסַת יְדֵי אָדָם וּמוּתָּר,
phrases.english: is that people did not make them, and they are permitted;

phrases.aramaic: אַף כׇּל שֶׁאֵין בָּהֶן תְּפִיסַת יְדֵי אָדָם וּמוּתָּר.
phrases.english: so too, anything that people did not make is permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְחָזַר הַדִּין, לֹא רְאִי זֶה כִרְאִי זֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After both single-case proofs were weakened, this step joins them into one combined proof.
steps.raayaObject: Worshipped stones that broke off a mountain are permitted.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The common feature of a worshipped mountain and a worshipped animal: neither was made by people, and both are permitted.

steps.title: Both cases are still in their natural state
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא attacks the combined proof: the mountain and the animal share another feature. Both are unchanged from how they were created, while the stones were broken off and changed.
steps.simpleTranslation: What about the common feature between them? They share something else: they were not changed from how they were created!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the הצד השוה proof. It finds a second feature the mountain and animal share, which the stones do not have.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A הצד השוה only works if the shared feature we picked is the only thing the two cases have in common. Here both the mountain and the animal are still in their original, natural form. The stones broke off the mountain, so they did change, and maybe that is why they should be forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: from how they were created; from their natural state

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new attack on just one case. It attacks the whole combined proof by showing the two cases share a second feature that the stones lack.

phrases.english: What about the common feature between them?
They are different, since they were not changed from how they were created!
phrases.notes: The stones are different: they broke off the mountain, so they are no longer in their original state.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָה לְהַצַּד הַשָּׁוֶה שֶׁבָּהֶן, שֶׁכֵּן לֹא נִשְׁתַּנּוּ מִבְּרִיָּיתָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the הצד השוה built in step 20.
steps.kashyaTarget: The combined proof from a mountain and an animal.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Both source cases are unchanged from their natural state, while the stones have changed. So the shared feature might be the real reason they are permitted, and it does not apply to the stones.

steps.title: Use a blemished animal and a mountain instead
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא fixes the proof by swapping in a בהמה בעלת מום. A blemished animal has changed from its natural state and is still permitted, so 'unchanged' is no longer a shared feature.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is learned from a blemished animal and from a mountain.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rebuilds the הצד השוה with a different pair: a blemished animal and a mountain. This gets around the challenge of step 21.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A בהמה בעלת מום is no longer in its original, perfect state, because it got a blemish. Yet it is permitted after being worshipped. So the pair no longer shares 'unchanged from creation', and their only common feature is that people did not make them. That feature applies to the stones, so the stones are permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: rather; we drop the old version and offer a new one
having a blemish; a blemished animal

steps.whatToRemember: The lenient view is proven through a הצד השוה: a blemished animal and a mountain are both permitted after being worshipped, and their only shared feature is that people did not make them. So stones that broke off a mountain, which people also did not make, are permitted too.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אָתְיָא מִבְּהֵמָה בַּעֲלַת מוּם, וּמֵהַר.
phrases.english: Rather, it is learned from a blemished animal and from a mountain.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָתְיָא מִבְּהֵמָה בַּעֲלַת מוּם, וּמֵהַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 21 by replacing the ordinary animal with a blemished animal.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rebuilding the proof by swapping one source case for a better one.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The mountain and the animal might be permitted only because they are unchanged from their natural state.
steps.terutzMaskana: A blemished animal has changed and is still permitted, so the only real common feature is no human involvement, and the stones are permitted.

steps.title: Another pair for the combined proof: an unblemished animal and a dried-up tree
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא offers a different pair of cases to build the same combined proof: a בהמה תמה and an אילן יבש. Both stay permitted after being worshipped.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or, if you like, prove it from an unblemished animal and from a dried-up tree.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second way to build the combined proof that the broken-off stones are permitted. This time it uses a healthy animal and a dried-up tree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each case alone has a weakness. A בהמה תמה is alive and unchanged from its natural state. A dried-up tree is not alive and has changed by withering, yet it is still permitted. A dried-up tree is attached to the ground, but an animal is not attached and is still permitted. What the two share is that neither was made by people, so the stones, which also were not made by people, stay permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: Or alternatively; another way to say it

steps.whatToRemember: The rule behind every version of the combined proof is the same: something not made by people does not become forbidden just because it was worshipped.

phrases.english: Or alternatively,
from an unblemished animal
and from a dried-up tree.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second pair of cases that avoids the 'unchanged' problem raised in step 21, alongside the fix in step 22.
steps.raayaObject: The broken-off stones of a worshipped mountain are permitted.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A combined proof from a worshipped בהמה תמה and a worshipped אילן יבש, both of which are permitted.

steps.title: Why does the other opinion forbid the stones?
steps.stepSummary: After so many proofs that the stones are permitted, the גמרא asks what reason the opinion that forbids them could have.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the one who forbids them, what is his reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets up its next move. It asks how the other side can forbid the stones when the logic seems to permit them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The combined proofs seem strong, so the opinion that forbids now needs explaining. The גמרא is not asking which proof is right. It wants to know what source could override that logic.

phrases.english: And the one who forbids?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from the proofs that permit to the opposing opinion.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What is the source or reason of the opinion that forbids the broken-off stones?

steps.title: The פסוק says not to permit it even when logic would
steps.stepSummary: The one who forbids learns from 'שקץ תשקצנו ותעב תתעבנו' that even when logic leads to permitting something connected to עבודה זרה, we must not permit it.
steps.simpleTranslation: For this purpose it is written: 'You shall utterly detest it and utterly abhor it.' Even though logic leads to permitting it, do not derive that.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. The one who forbids admits the logic points toward permitting, but he says a פסוק tells us not to follow that logic here.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The doubled wording 'שקץ תשקצנו... תעב תתעבנו' is read as an extra warning to stay far from עבודה זרה. So even a strong logical proof, like the combined proof, is not enough to permit the stones. The disagreement is about whether logic may be used here at all, not whether the logic works.
steps.confusionAlert: The one who forbids does not say the combined proof is wrong. He agrees the logic leads to permitting, but holds that the פסוק blocks using that logic for עבודה זרה.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that with עבודה זרה, a פסוק can tell us to be stricter than ordinary reasoning would be.

phrases.english: For this it is written:
"You shall utterly detest it
and you shall utterly abhor it,"
meaning that even though it comes
by logic to being permitted,
do not derive it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 24.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק 'שקץ תשקצנו ותעב תתעבנו' teaches that we must not permit something by logic in this area, so the stones stay forbidden.

steps.title: Trying to show that בני רבי חייא are the ones who permit
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tries to show which side of the argument בני רבי חייא hold. It brings חזקיה's question about someone who stood up an egg in order to bow to it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let us conclude that the sons of רבי חייא are the ones who permit, since חזקיה asked: if someone stood up an egg in order to bow to it, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets up a proof about who holds which view. It quotes חזקיה (one of רבי חייא's sons) asking about an egg that was stood up for worship.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier the argument was given between בני רבי חייא and רבי יוחנן without saying who holds what. Here the גמרא brings חזקיה's question as evidence. The next step explains how the question proves it.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it be concluded; it seems we can prove
The sons of רבי חייא (חזקיה and רבי יהודה)

phrases.english: Let it be concluded
that it is the sons of Rabbi Chiya who permit,
phrases.notes: Permit the boulder that broke off the worshipped mountain on its own.

phrases.english: since Chizkiya asked:
if someone stood up an egg in order to bow to it,
what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the reasoning of each side to identifying which רבנים hold which side.
steps.raayaObject: בני רבי חייא are the ones who permit the boulder.
steps.raayaSupportSource: חזקיה's question about a person who stood up an egg in order to bow to it.

steps.title: How the egg question proves that בני רבי חייא permit
steps.stepSummary: חזקיה is unsure only whether standing up the egg counts as a human act. That means without a human act, bowing alone would not forbid the egg. So בני רבי חייא hold that something not made by people, like the boulder, stays permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: You would assume he means he stood it up to bow to it and then bowed to it. His question is whether standing it up counts as an act or not. But if he had not stood it up, it would not become forbidden. Learn from this that the sons of רבי חייא are the ones who permit.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the proof from the egg. It finishes by concluding that בני רבי חייא are the ones who permit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: חזקיה's only doubt is whether standing up the egg counts as a human act (מעשה). That shows he holds that without any human act, worshipping an object does not forbid it. The boulder broke off with no human act, so חזקיה and his brother would permit it.

keyTerms.meaning: You would assume; it enters your mind
A human act or action done to the object
Learn from it; we can conclude

steps.confusionAlert: The words 'קא סלקא דעתך' tell you this is how we first understand חזקיה's question. Notice that the whole proof depends on reading the case this way.
steps.whatToRemember: This proof depends on reading חזקיה's case as one where the man also bowed to the egg. The next step rejects that reading, so it does not end up proving what בני רבי חייא hold.

phrases.english: You would assume
that he stood it up to bow to it, and he then bowed to it,
and his question is
whether this standing it up counts as an act
or does not count as an act,
but if he had not stood it up, it would not become forbidden.
Learn from this
that the sons of Rabbi Chiya are the ones who permit.

steps.triggerLanguage: קָא סָלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ לְהִשְׁתַּחֲווֹת לָהּ, וְהִשְׁתַּחֲוָה לָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how חזקיה's question in step 26 proves the point.
steps.raayaObject: בני רבי חייא hold that an object not touched by a human act is not forbidden by worship.
steps.raayaSupportSource: חזקיה is unsure only about whether standing up the egg counts as an act, so with no act at all the egg would clearly not be forbidden.

steps.title: Rejecting the proof by reading the egg case differently
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says the egg question proves nothing about בני רבי חייא. Maybe they forbid what was bowed to, and חזקיה's case is one where the egg was stood up but never bowed to.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, really I can tell you that בני רבי חייא are the ones who forbid. If a person bowed to the egg, it is forbidden even if he never stood it up. Here we are dealing with a person who stood up an egg in order to bow to it, but never actually bowed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא knocks down the proof from step 27. It explains חזקיה's question in a new way, so that it no longer tells us what בני רבי חייא hold.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 27 we read חזקיה as saying that bowing alone does not forbid. Now the גמרא says bowing alone surely does forbid, even without standing the egg up. חזקיה's doubt was about the opposite case: standing it up with no bowing at all. So the egg case cannot show that בני רבי חייא permit the boulder.

keyTerms.meaning: Really, I can tell you (the opposite of what you assumed)
He bowed down (an act of worship)
What case are we dealing with?

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two acts. 'Standing up' (זקף) is getting the egg ready. 'Bowing' (השתחוה) is the actual worship. This step says bowing alone already forbids; the open question is only about standing it up without bowing.

phrases.english: No, really I can tell you:
the sons of Rabbi Chiyya are the ones who forbid,

phrases.aramaic: דְּהִשְׁתַּחֲוָה לָהּ, אַף עַל גַּב דְּלֹא זְקָפָהּ אֲסוּרָה,
phrases.english: so if he bowed to it, even though he did not stand it up, it is forbidden;
and here, what case are we dealing with?
Where he stood up an egg in order to bow to it,
but he did not bow to it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof in step 27 by giving חזקיה's question a different case.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof that בני רבי חייא permit something not made by people
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed חזקיה's case involved bowing. It can be read as standing the egg up without any bowing, which says nothing about whether bowing forbids.

steps.title: Which opinion would have this doubt?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks who could be unsure about an egg that was stood up but not bowed to. One opinion clearly forbids it, and the other clearly permits it.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to whom is this question asked? If it follows the one who says a Jew's idol is forbidden right away, then the egg is forbidden. If it follows the one who says it is not forbidden until it is worshipped, then he never worshipped it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the new reading from step 28. Neither known opinion leaves room for a doubt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is an argument about a Jew's idol. One view says it is forbidden the moment it is set up. The other says it is forbidden only once it is actually worshipped. Under the first view the egg is clearly forbidden. Under the second it is clearly permitted, since no one bowed. So חזקיה's question has no room under either view.

phrases.english: And according to whom?
If according to the one who says:

phrases.aramaic: עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל אֲסוּרָה מִיָּד —
phrases.english: an idol belonging to a Jew is forbidden right away —
then it is forbidden;
if according to the one who says: not until it is worshipped —
but he did not worship it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the case suggested in step 28.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that חזקיה asked about an egg stood up but not bowed to
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Under both known opinions about a Jew's idol, the answer is obvious. So there is nothing to ask.

steps.title: The real case: a גוי bowed to the egg
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the case is a Jew who stood up the egg and a גוי who later bowed to it.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, the question is needed for this case: he stood up an egg in order to bow to it, he did not bow to it, and then a גוי came and bowed to it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the case so that חזקיה's question makes sense. Now the egg was stood up by a Jew but worshipped by a גוי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Adding the גוי's bowing gives the case real worship. It also brings in a Jew's act of setting the egg up. Whether these two together forbid the egg is a real question, as the next steps explain.

keyTerms.meaning: No, it is needed for (this specific case)

phrases.english: No, it is needed
for a case where he stood up an egg in order to bow to it,
and he did not bow to it,
and a non-Jew came and bowed to it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 29 by changing the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The case was a Jew who stood up the egg, with no worship at all.
steps.terutzMaskana: The case is a Jew who stood it up and a גוי who bowed to it.

steps.title: שמואל's ruling about a brick
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings שמואל's ruling: if a Jew stood up a brick to bow to it and a גוי bowed to it, the brick is forbidden. חזקיה's question builds on this.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is like what רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: a Jew who stood up a brick in order to bow to it, and a גוי came and bowed to it, the brick is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings an earlier ruling that the egg question rests on. This sets up חזקיה's actual question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל rules that a Jew's standing up a brick, together with a גוי's bowing, forbids the brick. So we already know the rule for a brick. חזקיה's question will be whether an egg is the same.

keyTerms.meaning: Like this ruling that was said

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הָא דְּאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל:
phrases.english: Like what רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל:
A Jew who stood up a brick in order to bow to it,
and a non-Jew came and bowed to it —
it is forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הָא דְּאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the source ruling that the case in step 30 is built on.
steps.raayaObject: That a Jew standing something up plus a גוי bowing to it can forbid it
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב יהודה in the name of שמואל, about a brick

steps.title: Is an egg like a brick?
steps.stepSummary: חזקיה asks whether only a brick becomes forbidden, since its standing position is easy to notice, or an egg too.
steps.simpleTranslation: And he was unsure: is it only a brick, whose standing position is noticeable, but not an egg? Or maybe there is no difference?
steps.whatsHappening: Now we finally hear חזקיה's real question. Does שמואל's brick rule also apply to an egg?
steps.deeperAnalysis: A brick standing on its end is clearly noticeable, so it shows that someone set it up on purpose. An egg standing up may not stand out the same way. The question is whether that difference matters.

phrases.english: And he was unsure:
phrases.notes: 'He' is חזקיה, whose egg question we have been explaining.

phrases.english: is it a brick, whose being stood up is noticeable,
but an egg — not?
Or perhaps there is no difference?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: States חזקיה's question using שמואל's brick ruling as the starting point.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether שמואל's brick rule applies to an egg, whose standing position is less noticeable.

steps.title: The question is left unanswered
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא leaves חזקיה's question unresolved.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it stand unresolved.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא ends the discussion without an answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No source decides whether an egg is like a brick, so the question stays open. Because of the new reading of the case, the egg question no longer tells us what בני רבי חייא hold.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it stand: the question stays unresolved

steps.whatToRemember: The proof about בני רבי חייא falls away. חזקיה's question was really about a Jew who stood up an egg and a גוי who bowed to it. שמואל rules a brick in that case is forbidden. Whether an egg is the same stays תיקו.

phrases.english: Let it stand unresolved.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the question from step 32 without an answer.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Whether a Jew standing up an egg plus a גוי bowing to it forbids the egg is left unresolved.

steps.title: Can stones from a worshiped mountain be used for the altar?
steps.stepSummary: רמי בר חמא asks whether the stones of a mountain that someone bowed to may be used to build the מזבח.
steps.simpleTranslation: רמי בר חמא asked: if someone bows down to a mountain, may its stones be used for the altar?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new question. רמי בר חמא wants to know if stones from a mountain that was worshiped can be used to build the מזבח.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A mountain is attached to the ground, so bowing to it does not make it forbidden in the usual way. The question is whether the מזבח needs a higher standard. Maybe stones from something that was worshiped are still not fit for holy use, even if they are otherwise permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: He asks, raises a question that needs an answer
The altar in the בית המקדש

steps.confusionAlert: The question is not whether the stones are forbidden for ordinary use. It is only about using them for the מזבח.

phrases.english: Rami bar Ḥama asked:
One who bows down to a mountain,
what is the law about using its stones for the altar?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After חזקיה's question is left unresolved, the גמרא moves on to a new question about worshiped mountains.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Are stones from a mountain that someone bowed to fit for building the מזבח, even though the mountain itself is not forbidden?
